scenes.heading: Vaccines
scenes.sub: How to beat a disease without catching it first
scenes.say: What if your immune system could practise fighting a disease before you ever caught it? That's exactly what a vaccine does. Vaccines have made diseases like polio and measles rare in many countries.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A practice match teaches a team the opponent's moves
scenes.science: A vaccine shows the immune system a pathogen's antigens
scenes.breaks: players remember by thinking; memory cells don't think, there are just more of them ready to divide.
scenes.say: A vaccine is like a practice match before the grand final. It shows your immune system the antigens of a pathogen with nothing at stake, without causing the full disease. When the real pathogen arrives, your body already knows the game plan.

scenes.heading: How a vaccine works
points: B cells make antibodies and memory cells
scenes.say: A vaccine contains antigens, or instructions to make them, not antibodies. Your own B cells make the antibodies and, importantly, memory cells. Active, because your body does the work. Artificial, because a vaccine triggered it.

scenes.heading: Primary vs secondary response
scenes.say: The vaccine triggers the primary response safely. It's slow and small. When the real pathogen arrives, memory cells give a secondary response: faster, bigger and longer lasting. A booster dose keeps memory cell numbers up.

scenes.heading: Herd immunity
scenes.everyday: A firebreak stops flames jumping to the next area
scenes.science: Immune people stop a pathogen jumping to new hosts
scenes.breaks: people move and mix, so herd immunity needs a high enough proportion immune. Measles needs a very high proportion.
scenes.say: Herd immunity is like a firebreak in the bush. When most people are immune, the pathogen can't jump between hosts. That protects people who can't be vaccinated, like newborn babies.

scenes.heading: Vaccines vs antibiotics
scenes.say: Don't mix up vaccines and antibiotics. Vaccines prevent disease by training your immune system. Antibiotics treat an existing infection by killing bacteria. Antibiotics are for bacteria only, so they won't fix a cold or the flu.

scenes.heading: How resistance spreads
steps: A few bacteria have a chance mutation
Most of the population is resistant
scenes.say: Antibiotic resistance spreads by natural selection. By chance, a few bacteria have a mutation that lets them survive. The antibiotic kills the rest. The resistant ones reproduce, until most are resistant. The antibiotic doesn't cause the mutation. And it's the bacteria that become resistant, not the person.

Quick recap. Vaccines carry antigens so memory cells form. The secondary response is faster, bigger and longer. Herd immunity protects others. Antibiotics only work on bacteria, and overuse speeds up resistance. Now try the practice questions!
